opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I come back to a lot. I think the honest answer is that there's a ceiling, and it's probably lower than people who are excited about simulation would like to believe, but higher than skeptics assume.

One way I think about it: even the person themselves can't perfectly predict what they'll do. If you ask me today how I'd answer a survey question two weeks from now, there's a meaningful chance I'd answer differently. In our work, when we built generative agents based on interviews with real people, we found it really useful to benchmark against that. We'd have participants take the same surveys and experiments twice, a couple of weeks apart, and measure how consistent they were with themselves. That self-consistency becomes a kind of practical upper bound. If an agent predicts your answers about as well as you predict your own future answers, it's hard to say it should do much better, because the remaining variance isn't really signal we're missing. Some of it is just noise, mood, context, what you had for breakfast.

So I'd split the problem into two parts. There's the reducible part: what we don't capture because our models or our data about the person are incomplete. Richer interviews, better models, and more context all chip away at that. Then there's the irreducible part, the stochasticity that's genuinely in human behavior, and also the fact that people change over time. You're not the same person a year from now, and new experiences reshape you in ways nobody could have forecast.

I also think the limit depends heavily on what you're predicting. Aggregate behavior, how a population might respond to a policy or a message, is much more predictable than one person's specific choice on a given afternoon. Individual noise averages out. So for many of the applications I care about, like social science and policy testing, you don't need to hit the theoretical limit on every individual for the simulation to be really valuable.

And there's a philosophical point: if we could predict someone perfectly, that would say something uncomfortable about agency. I don't think we're anywhere close, and I'm not sure we should want to be. The goal for me isn't perfect prediction. It's building models faithful enough to help us reason about people, while being clear-eyed about where that faithfulness breaks down.

r001.rationale: The response identifies irreducible stochasticity in human behavior, including mood and context, as noise that limits prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, and the honest answer is that there's a ceiling, and the ceiling is partly the point.

Human behavior isn't fully deterministic from the outside. If I ask you the same question twice, a week apart, you'll answer a bit differently. Your mood, what you ate, something you read that morning, all of it moves you. So when we build these generative agents and measure how well they predict a person, we don't compare against some perfect oracle. We compare against the person replicating themselves. We ask the same people the same survey two weeks later and see how consistent they are with their own earlier answers. That self-consistency is the practical ceiling. You can't reasonably expect a model to predict you better than you predict you.

What I find interesting is that the ceiling isn't the same everywhere. For something like the General Social Survey, attitudes about religion or politics, people are pretty stable, and the agents get quite close to that replication rate. For personality measures, also fairly good. But for behavior in economic games, where there's strategy and noise and a partner you're reacting to, both humans and agents get less consistent. So the limit moves depending on how much of the behavior is really "you" versus situational randomness.

Then there's a deeper question about what information even bears on the prediction. A lot of earlier work tried to predict people from demographics. Age, gender, race, income. And that gets you somewhere, but it also flattens people into stereotypes, and in our work it was clearly worse than giving the model a two-hour interview where the person talks about their life in their own words. The interview captures the idiosyncratic stuff, the reasons behind the attitudes, not just the category you fall into. So part of the theoretical limit is really an information limit. How much of a person's decision process can you actually elicit and encode?

And I'd add one more thing. Even if the limit were higher, I'm not sure we'd want to push all the way to it. The goal, at least for me, isn't to build a perfect copy of a specific person that can be used to anticipate what they'll do. It's to build simulations good enough that social scientists and policymakers can test ideas, pilot interventions, explore counterfactuals, before touching real people. For that, you need fidelity on the aggregate and on the structure of individual differences. You don't need to predict what Joon will have for lunch tomorrow. So I think of the limit less as a wall to break through and more as a calibration. It tells you where the model is trustworthy, and where it's just making things up.

r001.rationale: The response says human behavior is not fully deterministic and varies with factors such as mood and situational randomness, identifying randomness as a limit on prediction.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by predicting human behavior. If the goal is to predict exactly what someone will do in every possible situation, I’m skeptical that’s achievable. People respond to circumstances that we may not observe, and even the person themselves might not know what they’re going to do until they’re in that situation.

But that’s different from asking whether we can predict meaningful patterns. We might not know exactly what one person will do, but we could still estimate how likely different responses are, or how a group might respond to a change in their environment.

So I would frame the goal less as perfect prediction and more as understanding where prediction is useful and where uncertainty remains. And there’s a distinction between a theoretical limit and the limits of our models: if a model gets something wrong, that doesn’t necessarily mean human behavior is fundamentally unpredictable. It might just mean we haven’t captured the relevant context.

r001.rationale: The response questions exact prediction and points to unobserved circumstances and uncertainty, but it does not identify randomness in human behavior as a source of a theoretical limit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by predicting human behavior. If you mean predicting exactly what a particular person will do at a particular moment, there are fundamental limits. People respond to context, and we’re never going to observe every part of that context. And people change, so even a very rich account of someone’s past isn’t a complete description of their future.

But I don’t think perfect prediction is the right bar. We can ask whether a model captures useful patterns: how someone might respond to a question, or how a group might respond to a change in their environment. Those are probabilistic predictions, and we should evaluate them as such.

So I’d distinguish between building an oracle and building a useful scientific model. The latter can help us understand human behavior while still being explicit about uncertainty and where the model breaks down.

r001.rationale: The response describes limits from unobserved context and people changing, but does not identify randomness in human behavior as a source of the limit. Calling predictions probabilistic does not establish that point.
